extracted.intended_audience: editors, editorial staff, and policy-makers of peer-reviewed biomedical/medical journals (also authors and reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating, implementing, and enforcing conflict-of-interest (COI) policies for peer-reviewed medical/biomedical journals, covering definition, disclosure, management, and enforcement for authors, reviewers, and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear definition the journal uses as to what is conflict of interest and who is captured in the definition. Sample definition: conflict of interest exists when a participant in the publication process (author, peer reviewer or editor) has a competing interest that could unduly influence (or be reasonably seen to do so) his or her responsibilities in the publication process (submission of manuscripts, peer review, editorial decisions, and communication between authors, reviewers and editors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should articulate who is covered (authors, reviewers, editors) and specify the publication-process activities that could be influenced (submission, peer review, editorial decisions, communications). Clarity of definition is essential so those involved understand what must be disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of competing interests (required examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear statement of examples of the types of competing interests (and their definitions) the journal says must be declared. Should include the following as examples but there could be others: (I) Financial ties (II) Academic commitments (III) Personal relationships (IV) Political or religious beliefs (V) Institutional affiliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples and definitions of what competing interests should be declared. Recognize a wide range of competing interests and that multiple types can coexist; move beyond listing only financial conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaring conflicts: what, when, to whom, and format
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear statements on: (I) what is to be declared, when and to whom; (II) format for declaration; (III) a journal’s role in asking additional questions or seeking clarification about disclosures; and, (IV) consequences for failing to disclose before or after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals rely on declarants because routine monitoring is not possible, creating an onus on the declarer. Design disclosure questions to maximize likelihood of reporting relevant conflicts, specify formats (forms/statements), timelines (submission, revision, pre-publication), and who receives the disclosure (editor, editorial office).

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear statement on how conflict of interest will be managed by the journal, including the position that all relevant conflict of interest disclosures (or the declaration of no conflict of interest) will be published with the article and clarity about what conflict of interest situations will result in a manuscript not being considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe possible management actions (e.g., disclosure only, exclusion from review, editorial recusal, rejection) and explicitly state which situations lead to non-consideration. Make these rules known to authors, reviewers, and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish disclosures with every article
rubrics_metrics.description: All relevant author disclosures (or declaration of no conflict of interest) will be published with the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers need transparency; publishing disclosures is a central element of management. Journals should routinely include disclosure statements in the published record rather than hide them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-financial conflicts and clinical income
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand the scope of competing interests beyond financial ties to include non-financial conflicts (intellectual passion, personal relationships, political or religious beliefs, institutional affiliations) and effects of clinical income (e.g., physicians whose livelihood depends on certain procedures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the potential bias from scholarly commitments ('intellectual passion'), relationships, beliefs, institutional loyalties, and clinical income; provide examples and request that these be disclosed alongside financial ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of all participants (authors, reviewers, editors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Address conflicts threatening all participants in the research and publication continuum, including authors, peer reviewers, and editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should explicitly include reviewers and editors (not only authors) and state expectations and disclosure requirements for each role. Note that conflicts between editors and journal owners are a related area (see separate WAME policy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility to investigate and act on undisclosed conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors have a responsibility for investigating, and if relevant acting, if competing interests surface after a manuscript is submitted or published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take allegations of failure to declare seriously; outline investigation procedures and possible post-publication actions (correction, retraction, notice). Specify consequences for nondisclosure and processes for response.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single universal standard — allow journal-specific operational definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: WAME did not prescribe a universal standard for when meaningful conflict of interest exists; it defined and recommended elements of COI policies and encouraged journals to establish their own standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give journals latitude to set operational definitions and thresholds appropriate to their context, discipline, and culture; WAME offers factors to consider rather than absolute rules. Avoid overly broad exhaustive lists that could paralyze publication processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on full written disclosure as the backbone
rubrics_metrics.description: The backbone of managing conflicts of interest is full written disclosure; without it, nothing else is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize disclosure is imperfect but necessary. Even with disclosure, editors must still determine whether a conflict is sufficient to impair objectivity; policies should state how that judgment will be made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design disclosures to maximize accurate reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should ask about conflict of interest in such a way that there will be a high likelihood of reporting relevant conflict of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific, structured questions rather than vague prompts; follow up for clarification when needed; impose an onus on declarants to report carefully and comprehensively.

rubrics_metrics.name: State consequences for failing to disclose
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify consequences for failing to disclose before or after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe sanctions or remedial actions (corrections, retractions, bans, notices) and implement procedures for investigation and decision-making when nondisclosure is identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make COI policies public and accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should make these policies readily accessible to everyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish policies on journal websites and include them in author/reviewer guidance so stakeholders understand expectations; tailor policies to best standards of the discipline and local context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance comprehensiveness with feasibility in governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive concern or excessively comprehensive lists of possible competing interests could paralyze the peer review and publication process; editors must make judgments as to the strength of the conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide factors to guide editorial judgment about severity and manageability of conflicts; insist on uncensored information to permit informed decisions rather than attempting to enumerate every conceivable conflict.
